claims.text: Ten hours of high-energy ball milling followed by SPS at 900–1000 °C, a heating rate above 100 °C/min, and a dwell below 5 minutes will produce greater than 98% theoretical density in CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed milling and SPS process will produce a 20–50 nm grain size.
The processed CoCrFeNiTi will be a dual-phase solid solution dominated by FCC with a minor BCC fraction.
A rapid SPS thermal cycle will suppress diffusion-driven brittle HCP formation by limiting the time available for Ti-driven HCP nucleation.
Rapid SPS will suppress Laves and other complex intermetallic phases.
CoCrFeNiTi has sufficiently high stacking-fault energy at 900–1000 °C to help stabilize FCC over HCP.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the FCC phase of CoCrFeNiTi against HCP in the proposed temperature window.
Solute drag helps stabilize the nanocrystalline FCC/BCC matrix.
Grain-boundary strengthening and Ti-related solute strengthening together will produce a hardness of 450–550 HV.
The 900–1000 °C window is below the threshold for significant grain coarsening and Laves-phase precipitation.
Keeping displacement below 10 µm/s during heating will prevent excessive thermal-expansion mismatch.
Longer milling increases contamination and oxide or carbide formation even when a protective atmosphere is used.
Milling beyond 15 hours is the failure threshold for excessive contamination and oxide formation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Sintering above 1100 °C causes grain coarsening and HCP or Laves-phase precipitation.
Slow cooling permits HCP nucleation and destroys the proposed dual-phase stability.
The processed alloy will have a compressive yield strength above 1500 MPa.
FCC dominance will provide ductility above 10%.
Conventional casting produces a porous, coarse-grained, homogeneous single-phase CoCrFeNiTi alloy with hardness below 200 HV.
Annealing the processed alloy at 1100 °C for one hour will increase its grain size above 1 µm while maintaining its composition.
If the annealed coarse-grained sample remains statistically as hard as the nanocrystalline sample and above 450 HV, grain refinement as the primary hardness mechanism is falsified.
